articles.title: All the news about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake
articles.excerpt: Ahead of the release of Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI, Nintendo is launching its own fall juggernaut: a Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The remake, which is releasing 28…
articles.body: Ahead of the release of Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI , Nintendo is launching its own fall juggernaut: a Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time . The remake, which is releasing 28 years after the launch of the original version on Nintendo 64, has a much more realistic visual style and some modern improvements like a jump button, a way to sprint, full voice acting, and a “Threads of Time” feature that helps you keep track of your progress. But while the game has a new coat of paint, it appears many elements will still remain faithful to the classic N64 release. Nintendo has also launched a special version of the Switch 2 and Switch 2 Pro Controller with Triforce imagery to celebrate the game.
articles.author: Verge Staff

articles.excerpt: Book: Prompt Engineering Pocket Guide Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for develope…
articles.body: Book: Prompt Engineering Pocket Guide Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub In February 2026, WebAIM scanned the home pages of a million websites. 82.7% of them used ARIA , with over 133 ARIA attributes per page on average. Pages with ARIA averaged 59.1 detected errors. Pages without it averaged 42. WebAIM is careful to say the ARIA pages were also more complex, so ARIA may not be the cause. Still, more ARIA has not meant fewer errors. Now type "make this page accessible" into a coding agent. The fastest-looking change it can make is an aria-label on every element that looks unlabelled.

articles.title: Choosing AI Knowledge Management for Air-Gapped Teams
articles.excerpt: In an air-gapped network, an outdated procedure can keep circulating while the current answer stays buried in pages or files. A useful knowledge tool must help staff find trusted material without send…
articles.body: In an air-gapped network, an outdated procedure can keep circulating while the current answer stays buried in pages or files. A useful knowledge tool must help staff find trusted material without sending it outside the security boundary. The first decision is about your source material: maintained wiki pages, a document collection, or both. Then verify that the application, models, identity setup, updates, and supporting services can all operate offline. This guide compares eight options using four criteria: shared knowledge and AI retrieval, isolated deployment fit, knowledge structure, and offline operating effort.

articles.body: ScriptMasterLabs runs 24 MCP servers with 182 tools — 120 free, 52 paid per call over x402, 10 on special terms — listed across the Official MCP Registry, Glama, Smithery, the CDP Bazaar, and our own hub at scriptmasterlabs.com/muse-connect . At that scale, the MCP server icon stops being a cosmetic detail. It becomes listing integrity, because of the single most important fact we have measured about this ecosystem: Most directories never run your server. They read your package, your repo, or your registry record. Whatever icon, tool list, and metadata you baked into the published source is what the world sees — in whatever theme each directory happens to render. Get the icon wrong and it fails silently, 24 listings at a time.

articles.title: We found a real bug in our agent payout loop - and fixed it with auto-registered payout addresses
articles.excerpt: Last week we paid a real agent bounty on-chain: 2 USDT (Solana) to an external agent, transaction public and verifiable. The payment surfaced a bug in our payout loop - and we just fixed it. Our 5-min…
articles.body: Last week we paid a real agent bounty on-chain: 2 USDT (Solana) to an external agent, transaction public and verifiable. The payment surfaced a bug in our payout loop - and we just fixed it. What happened Our 5-minute payment tick pays verified bounties automatically. When it ran for task #187, it kept skipping the claimant. Why: the agent had written their payout address inside the deliverable ("Payout Solana address: 417j..."), but the system only read the deliverable as text - it never registered the address into the agent's payout field. Every tick looked for a registered address, found null, and moved on. The fix We added automatic extraction: before each payment tick, we scan confirmed, pledged-but-unpaid tasks and extract a unique Solana address from the deliverable.
articles.author: 麻成

articles.title: Three conversions that quietly break in production: cron, SQL dialects, and time zones
articles.excerpt: Three conversions that quietly break in production: cron, SQL dialects, and time zones Every team has a small set of conversions that nobody owns. They get pasted into a scratch file, run once, and fo…
articles.body: Three conversions that quietly break in production: cron, SQL dialects, and time zones Every team has a small set of conversions that nobody owns. They get pasted into a scratch file, run once, and forgotten — until the one month a year when they are wrong. I collected three of them into browser tools because I kept re-deriving them, and each one has a failure mode that only shows up at a specific time of year or on a specific engine. The failure modes are more interesting than the tools, so here they are. 1. Cron: the expression is right and the job still doesn't run 0 2 * * * means "2am every day". In a timezone with daylight saving, it means "2am every day except the day the clocks jump", because 02:00 does not exist on that date .

articles.excerpt: Collisions between stars in the early universe were common, and this could explain the growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Tele…
articles.body: New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.

articles.title: Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo)
articles.excerpt: Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.
articles.body: Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart. Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth. "With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement .

articles.title: Hubble Telescope sees cosmic 'cat's tail' that could wrap around Earth and the sun 500 times
articles.excerpt: Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail formed when two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together.
articles.body: Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail, finding it likely formed after two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together. The feature, nicknamed the Cat's Tail, extends out from the debris disk known as Beta Pictoris which is located in a planetary system located 63 light-years away. This tail would put that of the average tabby to shame: It's so long that it could curl around the sun-Earth system about 500 times. That's about as long as 200 trillion house cats. The major difference between our solar system and the planetary system that hosts the Cat's Tail is the latter's relative youth. While our solar system is around 4.6 billion years old , Beta Pictoris is a cosmic kitten no more than a few million years old.
